title: Who Is Anupama Ramachandran? The Chennai Cueist Who Became the First Indian Woman to Win a World Snooker Title — and Just Defended It at Home
excerpt: Born in Chennai in 2002, Anupama Ramachandran chose snooker over chess at a Mylapore Club summer camp at 13, won a world under-16 title at 15, and in November 2025 became the first Indian woman to win the IBSF World Snooker Championship — then defended it in Indore on November 21, 2026, to become the first Indian to win back-to-back world snooker crowns, all while completing two postgraduate degrees.
body:
• Anupama Ramachandran, 24, born in Chennai on May 19, 2002, defended her IBSF World Snooker Championship title in Indore on November 21, 2026, beating Hong Kong China's So Man Yan 3–1 — the first Indian to win back-to-back world snooker crowns, according to The Bridge.
  • Her first title, in Doha on November 13, 2025, made her the first Indian woman to win the championship: she beat three-time champion Ng On-yee 3–2, potting the final black after Ng missed it with the score at 61–60 in the deciding frame.
  • She started at a Mylapore Club summer camp at 13, choosing snooker over chess; her family installed a table at home a year later and her father stepped back from his real-estate business to travel with her.
  • Alongside the two world titles she holds the 2023 Women's Snooker World Cup team title, the 2023 World Women's Under-21 title and the 2024 Asian championship, reached a career-high World Women's Snooker ranking of sixth — and has completed a Master of Commerce while pursuing a second postgraduate degree in public policy.

Anupama Ramachandran is the first Indian woman to win a world snooker championship — and, as of Saturday night in Indore, the first Indian of any kind to defend one. The 24-year-old from Chennai beat Hong Kong China's So Man Yan 3–1 in the final of the IBSF World Snooker Championship at the Yeshwant Club on November 21, 2026, a year after her maiden title in Doha. Winning once put her in the record books. Winning again, at home, made the record hers alone: no Indian had previously won back-to-back IBSF world snooker crowns. Our report of the final is here.

The defence in Indore

The final did not start her way. Anupama lost a scrappy opening frame 16–58, then found her rhythm and took control, according to The Bridge. She levelled the match 83–7, built on runs of 31, 19 and 16, moved ahead with an 85–26 frame, and closed out the title 65–37, potting a long blue to the bottom-right pocket and the pink to the top-right to seal it. She had reached the final with two 3–1 wins, over fellow Indian Keerthana Pandian in the quarter-finals and England's Tessa Davidson in the semi-finals, and the title earned her USD 4,000. Speaking after the event, she said defending the title was even more special than winning it the first time, and that doing it on home soil made it memorable.

The final black in Doha

The title she was defending had been won in the tightest way the sport allows. In Doha on November 13, 2025, Anupama faced Ng On-yee of Hong Kong China, a three-time world champion, in a best-of-five final that swung throughout: Ng took the first frame 74–51, Anupama levelled 65–41, Ng went ahead again 71–10, and a break of 29 helped Anupama take the fourth 78–20 to force a decider, according to her career record. In the deciding frame she led 61–42, but a safety attempt on the final green let Ng clear the colours from green to pink and close to 60–61. Ng then missed the final black. Anupama, taking a little longer over the shot than she normally does, potted it to win 68–60 and become the first Indian woman to win the championship. She had arrived in Doha straight from a Heyball World Championship in Australia, with one day at home in between, and had not felt like a champion at all in the early rounds.

"I knew no Indian woman had ever won an IBSF world title. But that wasn't something I carried into the final. I wanted to win for myself. The 'first Indian' part only hit me after the tournament was over."

— Anupama Ramachandran, writing in The Bridge after the Doha title

A summer camp in Mylapore

Anupama Ramachandran was born on May 19, 2002, in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, and attended Vidya Mandir Senior Secondary School. She was introduced to cue sports at 13 or 14 at a summer coaching camp at the Mylapore Club, where the choice was between chess and snooker. She picked snooker — and then did something her mother had never seen: she asked to continue after the camp ended. For months she played three days a week, two hours at a time, with the other camp children. Club members told her parents she had potential. After she finished runner-up in a Tamil Nadu state under-18 event in 2015, she began taking the sport seriously. In 2016 her family installed a snooker table at home, which she later said changed her entire trajectory, because it gave her hours of solo practice. Her father left his real-estate business to support her career and travel with her; her mother is a chartered accountant; and her uncle Narayanan trained the mental side of her game — staying calm and present while an opponent scores. She has no siblings and grew up in a joint family.

The long apprenticeship

The rise was steady rather than sudden. Anupama made her IBSF debut in Belgium in 2016, reaching the under-18 quarter-finals, and in October 2017 won the inaugural Girls' World Open Under-16 Championship in Saint Petersburg, beating Pandian 3–1 in the final. Through 2016 and 2017 she collected multiple Tamil Nadu state titles across the under-18, under-21 and senior categories, and the 2017 National Girls Under-18 title. At senior level the finals kept ending the same way for a while: runner-up to Amee Kamani at the Indian championship in December 2021, and runner-up at the IBSF World Under-21 Championship in Bucharest in August 2022, losing 1–4 to Thailand's Panchaya Channoi. Her early coach was N. Suryanarayanan; from 2018 she worked with former Indian player S. A. Saleem, who coached her by video call every day through the COVID-19 lockdown while she practised on the table at home.

Breakthrough: a World Cup, an Asian title, a ranking final

The international titles arrived in a rush from 2023. On her World Women's Snooker (WWS) tour debut at the 2023 Women's Snooker World Cup in Bangkok, she and Kamani, playing as India A, beat England A's Reanne Evans and Rebecca Kenna 4–3 in the final to win the team title. The same year she won the World Women's Under-21 Championship, coming from 1–2 down to beat two-time defending champion Ploychompoo Laokiatphong 3–2, was runner-up at the separate IBSF World Under-21 event in Riyadh, and reached the final of the IBSF women's Six-red World Championship in Doha, where Vidya Pillai beat her. She was a flag bearer for Tamil Nadu at the 2023 National Games in Goa, and in December 2023 won her first senior national title — in English billiards, recovering from two games down to beat Kamani 3–2. In July 2024 she won the Asian Women's Snooker Championship in Riyadh, beating Pandian 3–0 in the semi-finals and Channoi 3–1 in the final. The following month she reached her first WWS ranking final at the US Women's Open in Seattle, beating defending champion Mink Nutcharut and Kenna before losing 0–4 to Ng — the opponent she would beat for the world title fifteen months later. From 2023 she also trained abroad with former professional Nigel Bond, who she says changed how she thinks about strategy and pressure.

A student champion

Anupama has built this record alongside postgraduate study, not instead of it. She completed a Master of Commerce at M.O.P. Vaishnav College for Women in Chennai — her school and college both accommodated her tournament schedule — and by November 2025 was pursuing a second postgraduate degree, in public policy, at the same college. She won the women's snooker title at the 2024–25 Indian National Championships, reached a career-high WWS ranking of sixth in March 2025, and in 2026 received the Excellence in Sports Award at The Hindu World of Women Awards. Her career-high break of 119 was a record for an Indian woman as of March 2026. She is supported under the Tamil Nadu government's Mission International Medals Scheme. Her billiards game has kept pace with her snooker: she won the Indian women's billiards title again in January 2026, beating Kamani 197–112 the day after losing the snooker final to her, and won the billiards final at the 2026 Commonwealth Cue Sports Championships, beating Revanna Umadevi 213–159. In September 2026 she reached the semi-finals of the UK Women's Championship. In a 2024 WWS interview she described concentrating on each shot in turn as the strength of her game, and named Mark Selby and Judd Trump as her favourite players.

Why she matters

India has produced celebrated male cueists, but no Indian woman had won an IBSF world snooker title before Anupama — and the sport she plays carries stereotypes she pushes against directly: that snooker is only for rich people, or gambling, or something people do for fun in a club. Snooker, she says, is a competitive sport that requires precision, discipline and patience. For readers in the diaspora who follow Indian sport from abroad, her story is the other half of the Harmanpreet Kaur story from the same twelve months: two women from Chennai and Moga taking world titles in sports where India had never won them, and then backing the first title up rather than treating it as a peak. What she wants from the attention is specific, and she stated it herself in The Bridge: more leagues in India to raise the sport's profile, and more girls at the table.

"The only thing I hope for is that more girls take up this sport and believe they belong here."

— Anupama Ramachandran, in The Bridge

At 24, with two world titles, an Asian title and a World Cup team gold already won, the question for Anupama Ramachandran is no longer whether she belongs at the top of women's snooker. It is how long she stays there — and how many players follow her in.
